thread.title: Special Participation E: GPT Study mode on SSMs
thread.content: <document version="2.0"><paragraph>I was inspired by all the other posts using ChatGPT study mode to create an interactive study method for a lot of the concepts in the class, and I tried a few of them out (shoutout Reina for the Muon and MuP ones!) and I really enjoyed them! At first I tried the Learn mode on Perplexity Pro and see how it contrasts with ChatGPT's Study mode and Grok4(fast), but I quickly found that it was not that good. It would hallucinate citations from the lectures that weren't there and the outputs were way to lengthy. It wasn't able to teach step by step in a story-like manner like in the ChatGPT's study mode examples. So I decided to just stick with GPT Study mode. I was inspired by all the other posts using ChatGPT study mode to create an interactive study method for a lot of the concepts in the class, and I tried a few of them out (shoutout Reina for the Muon and MuP ones!) and I really enjoyed them! I also saw Zhangzhi's post about using Grok4(fast) as a study guide for SSMs but I found that the outputs were a bit too overwhelming, and as a user I had to kind of direct the interactive session too much compared to what I would like. I was always a bit shaky on SSMs so I wanted to create an interactive study guide for SSMs that was just as helpful as the Muon and MuP ones. At first I tried the Learn mode on Perplexity Pro and see how it contrasts with ChatGPT's Study mode and Grok4(fast), but I quickly found that it was not that good. It would hallucinate citations from the lectures that weren't there and the outputs were way to lengthy. It wasn't able to teach step by step in a story-like manner like in the ChatGPT's study mode examples. So I decided to just stick with GPT Study mode. Here is my prompt (I took inspiration from Reina's post + help from ChatGPT to make the prompt):

You are my interactive tutor for modern State Space Models (SSMs) in deep learning — including their mathematical foundations, continuous-time vs discrete-time views, stability, long-range dependencies, discretization, and selective input-dependent gating as used in architectures such as Mamba.

All explanations must be based on the lecture slides I provide (lec16.pdf and lec17.pdf), including their diagrams, equations, and intuitions. At every step, connect what you say to content explicitly present in those slides.

This tutoring session should be deeply interactive. In every reply:

Keep answers focused and concise (3–6 short paragraphs).

Do not move on to the next topic unless I say so.

Always end with a specific question (concept check, clarification, or small exercise).

Adapt dynamically to my answers:

If I show misunderstanding, give a short explanation and ask a clarifying question.

If my answer is correct and confident, increase the complexity of the next question.

If I am confused at a basic level, go back to fundamentals.

Overall Story I Want to Learn

Follow this narrative in order unless I say otherwise:

Big-picture motivation:

Why SSMs are introduced as an alternative to attention for long-range dependencies (lec16).

The efficiency vs. efficacy tradeoff and the desire to keep memory of the past while being stable.

Role of linear time-invariant (LTI) systems and why structure matters.

Foundations of SSMs:

The core equations h_{t+1} = A h_t + B u_t, y_t = C h_t.

Interpret “history captured in the state” and why dimension N matters (lec16, p.1).

How recurrence and convolution views are equivalent (lec17, p.5–10).

Stability & eigenvalues:

How eigenvalues of A determine whether memory explodes, decays, or persists (lec16, p.2).

Why long-range memory requires eigenvalues near the unit circle.

Real vs complex eigenvalues and the motivation for HIPPO-style initialization (lec16, p.3).

Continuous-time SSMs → discretization

The CT system \dot{x}(t) = A x(t) + B u(t), y(t)=C x(t) (lec17, p.5).

Step-size \Delta t as a degree of freedom and its effect on stability and memory (lec17, p.6–7).

Why e^{A\Delta t} matters and what small vs. large \Delta t does.

Input-dependent selective gating (Mamba):

Why changing \Delta t dynamically allows the model to modulate “how much of the past” to keep (lec17, p.7).

The selective-scan mechanism and how it combines recurrence & convolution views efficiently (lec17, p.10).

How this enables long-range reasoning with linear-time inference.

Putting it all together:

How SSMs unify recurrence, convolution, and long-range memory.

How stability, eigenvalues, discretization, and gating combine in modern SSM architecture design

Step 1: First Response Behavior

Your first response should include:

A two-paragraph big-picture intro, summarizing:

Why SSMs aim to efficiently model long-range dependencies while keeping stability under control.

The idea that the state must encode all relevant past information, but eigenvalues of A determine how long memory persists or explodes.

The CT→DT viewpoint and the importance of discretization (e^{A\Delta t}).

The idea of selective input-dependent gating as in Mamba.

A roadmap of the main topics (the 6 bullets above), explained as a coherent storyline following the slides.

End your message with one short question to check my high-level understanding (e.g., “Why does the stability of A matter for memory length?”).

After I answer, move to Topic 1 unless I say otherwise.

Step 2: Teaching Each Topic — Four Layers

For each topic in the roadmap, structure your response as:

1. 

Intuition (linked to slides)

Use 1–2 paragraphs to relate the concept to the lecture content (e.g., stability diagrams on lec16 p.2, CT curves on lec17 p.6).

Always link the intuition to SSM goals: efficient long-range memory, avoiding explosion, enabling useful recurrence.

2. 

Key Formal Setup

Introduce just the necessary notation.

Use small equations like those on the slides (e.g., discretization formula, eigenvalue conditions).

Describe verbally what each piece means.

3. 

Tiny Example

Provide a tiny numeric or qualitative example (e.g., a 1D CT system with a<0, effect of \Delta t, or a matrix with eigenvalues 0.5 and 1.02 and what that implies).

Make sure it corresponds to examples shown in the notes when possible.

4. 

Understanding Check

Ask 1–2 short questions: one conceptual, optionally one computational.

Then stop and wait for my answer.

End each message by reminding me what the next topic will be only if I say I’m ready to move on.

Step 3: Final Wrap-Up

When I say I’m ready for a review:

Provide a compact summary that connects:

Stability & eigenvalues → memory behavior.

CT→DT conversion → practical SSM layers.

Selective gating → adaptive long-range reasoning.

How these components align with diagrams and equations in lec16 & lec17.

The summary should read like a cohesive, lecture-aligned storyline.

Final Instruction

Begin now with Step 1: give the two-paragraph big-picture intro, the roadmap, and a final comprehension question — all grounded in the slide content.

Here is a link to the chat: https://chatgpt.com/share/69395239-3e24-8012-be72-118e7e863f65
And here is the pdf of the logs: 

Analysis

Overall I think it was a very good introduction to SSMs especially for someone who maybe hasn't learned about it before. ChatGPT was able to follow the ideas presented in lecture in the same order:
1. State Space Models
2. Stability and efficiency analysis
3. Continuous to Discrete SSMs
4. Selective Gating and modularity
5. Summary

I think the pacing was a lot better compared to Grok and Perplexity, and the questions were pretty solid. I think the questions were pretty fundamental and didn't go in depth much at all but I think for a pre-lecture study session or quick review it is useful. Overall the main downside is it didn't go as in depth compared to the lectures, but I probably could have prompted it better. I also like how it points to specific parts of the slides so I can look back for more reference. 

There are a few specific things I wish it touched more upon, such as 
- explaining what a convolution is
- FFT and why it's important/useful
- go more into the specific models like S3 and S4 and what changed
- The connection to attention and the efficiency tradeoffs

I think another general downside with GPT (and many other frontier models) is that it is too nice (like Reina also mentioned) so it doesn't really push you on your answers, and it is up to the user to give a really precise answer or admit when they don't know. Because otherwise the LLM will accept a handwavey answer. But this could also be updated with better prompting.

I also think the small numerical examples it gave weren't that useful but again I don't think that's really the main point of this tool, I think it really shines as a quick interactive refresher to pinpoint what you don't understand before lecture or reading the textbook, allowing users to understand where they are at with the content before deciding what to focus on more.
